set.seed(310)   # the deck's one seed: the split, then every random step below, in order
nh_id <- sample(nrow(nh))
nh_train <- nh[nh_id[1:4000], ]
nh_tune  <- nh[nh_id[4001:7000], ]
nh_test  <- nh[nh_id[7001:nrow(nh)], ]
# Simulated data for part 1: noise that grows with x, a bump at 3 (height 3, sd 0.2), and few rows with x between
# 4 and 6 (a quarter of the density elsewhere). The note uses the same simulation, and its first two samples are
# these two.
f_sim <- function(x) 3 + x + 2 * sin(x) + 3 * exp(-(x - 3)^2 / (2 * 0.2^2))
s_sim <- function(x) 0.5 + 0.35 * x
x_thin <- function(n) { u <- runif(n, 0, 8.5); case_when(u < 4 ~ u, u < 4.5 ~ 4 + 4 * (u - 4), TRUE ~ u + 1.5) }
sim <- function(n) tibble(x = x_thin(n)) |> mutate(y = f_sim(x) + s_sim(x) * rnorm(n))
het_train <- sim(1000)
het_fresh <- sim(7000)   # about 400 of them with x between 4 and 6
x_grid <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 201))
# The causality lecture's diagram of the adjustment theorem.
dag_adjust <- function(intervened = FALSE, title = NULL) {
  s <- if (intervened) '{ Z [pos="1,1"] T [pos="0,0"] Y [pos="2,0"] Z -> Y T -> Y }' else
                       '{ Z [pos="1,1"] T [pos="0,0"] Y [pos="2,0"] Z -> T Z -> Y T -> Y }'
  dag(s) %>% tidy_dagitty() %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
    geom_dag_point(size = 15, colour = "#e5ecf6") +
    geom_dag_text(size = 8, colour = v_dark) +
    geom_dag_edges(edge_width = 1.3) +
    expand_limits(x = c(-0.35, 2.35), y = c(-0.4, 1.45)) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme_dag_blank() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, hjust = 0.5, colour = v_dark))
}
# The explanatory causal model of part 4, drawn by hand in the convention of Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024),
# Figure 5: one graph with the outcome y and the prediction y-hat (boxed); solid arrows for relations in the
# world, dashed arrows from the model's inputs to the prediction, curved so that they cross no node.
ecm_plot <- function() {
  arw <- arrow(length = unit(0.13, "inches"), type = "closed")
  solid <- tribble(~x, ~y, ~xend, ~yend,          # x1 -> x2, x1 -> y, x2 -> y, x1 -> x3, y -> x3
    0.29, 1.15, 1.71, 1.95,   0.33, 1, 3.67, 1,   2.29, 1.95, 3.71, 1.15,   0.29, 0.85, 1.71, 0.05,   3.71, 0.85, 2.29, 0.05)
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = solid, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = v_dark, linewidth = 1.1, arrow = arw) +
    annotate("curve", x = 2.32, y = -0.2, xend = 5.05, yend = -0.85, colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dashed",
             curvature = 0.12, arrow = arw) +
    annotate("curve", x = 0, y = 0.64, xend = 5.0, yend = -1.05, colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dashed",
             curvature = 0.42, angle = 90, arrow = arw) +
    annotate("curve", x = 2.34, y = 2.15, xend = 5.4, yend = -0.55, colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dashed",
             curvature = -0.55, angle = 90, arrow = arw) +
    geom_label(data = tibble(x = c(0, 2, 4, 2), y = c(1, 2.1, 1, -0.1), lab = c("x[1]", "x[2]", "y", "x[3]")),
               aes(x, y, label = lab), parse = TRUE, size = 7, linewidth = 0.3, label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines")) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 5.1, xmax = 5.7, ymin = -1.2, ymax = -0.6, fill = "white", colour = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
    annotate("text", x = 5.4, y = -0.9, label = "hat(y)", parse = TRUE, size = 7) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.4, 5.9), ylim = c(-1.75, 2.5), clip = "off") + theme_void()
}

# Part 1: a line with constant noise, lm's 90% prediction interval, the points outside it highlighted.
bg2 <- tibble(x = runif(250, 0, 10)) |> mutate(y = 1 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(250))
bg2_fit <- lm(y ~ x, bg2)
bg2_band <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 101)) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(predict(bg2_fit, tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 101)), interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)))
bg2_pi <- predict(bg2_fit, bg2, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)
bg2$out <- bg2$y < bg2_pi[, "lwr"] | bg2$y > bg2_pi[, "upr"]
bg_save(ggplot(bg2, aes(x, y)) + geom_ribbon(data = bg2_band, aes(x, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "#fde725", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = bg2_band, aes(x, fit), colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +

# Part 4: the ECM for the protein-signalling data of Sachs et al. (2005), as drawn by Loftus, Bynum and Hansen
# (2024), Figure 5 (left): PKA and its descendants in bold; blue, the paths from PKA; dashed, the model's inputs.
sachs_nodes <- tribble(~name, ~x, ~y, ~bold,
  "PKC", 2, 4, FALSE, "pjnk", 3.5, 4, FALSE, "P38", 0.5, 3, TRUE, "praf", 2, 3, TRUE, "pmek", 3.5, 3, TRUE,
  "plcg", 0.5, 2, FALSE, "PKA", 2, 2, TRUE, "p44/42", 3.5, 2, FALSE, "pakts473", 2, 1.3, TRUE,
  "PIP2", 0.5, 0.6, FALSE, "PIP3", 2, 0.6, FALSE, "hat", 3.5, 0.6, FALSE)
sachs_edge <- function(from, to, kind, a = 0.22, b = 0.26) {
  f <- sachs_nodes[sachs_nodes$name == from, ]; t <- sachs_nodes[sachs_nodes$name == to, ]
  len <- sqrt((t$x - f$x)^2 + (t$y - f$y)^2)
  tibble(x = f$x + a * (t$x - f$x) / len, y = f$y + a * (t$y - f$y) / len,
         xend = t$x - b * (t$x - f$x) / len, yend = t$y - b * (t$y - f$y) / len, kind = kind)
}
sachs_solid <- bind_rows(
  sachs_edge("PKC", "pjnk", "world", 0.45, 0.4), sachs_edge("PKC", "P38", "world"), sachs_edge("PKC", "praf", "world"),
  sachs_edge("PKC", "pmek", "world"), sachs_edge("plcg", "PKC", "world"), sachs_edge("PIP2", "PKC", "world"),
  sachs_edge("PKA", "pjnk", "world"), sachs_edge("PKA", "p44/42", "world", 0.45, 0.5), sachs_edge("pmek", "p44/42", "world"),
  sachs_edge("plcg", "PIP2", "world"), sachs_edge("PIP3", "PIP2", "world", 0.4, 0.4), sachs_edge("PIP3", "pakts473", "world", 0.2, 0.2),
  sachs_edge("PKA", "P38", "pka"), sachs_edge("PKA", "praf", "pka"), sachs_edge("PKA", "pmek", "pka"),
  sachs_edge("PKA", "pakts473", "pka", 0.2, 0.2), sachs_edge("praf", "pmek", "pka", 0.45, 0.5))
sachs_dashed <- bind_rows(sachs_edge("P38", "hat", "pka", 0.35, 0.35) |> mutate(curv = 0.12),
  sachs_edge("praf", "hat", "pka", 0.3, 0.35) |> mutate(curv = 0.1), sachs_edge("pmek", "hat", "pka", 0.3, 0.35) |> mutate(curv = -0.35),
  sachs_edge("pakts473", "hat", "pka", 0.35, 0.45) |> mutate(curv = 0.05), sachs_edge("PKA", "hat", "direct", 0.35, 0.35) |> mutate(curv = 0.2))
sachs_arw <- arrow(length = unit(0.09, "inches"), type = "closed")
sachs_cols <- c(world = "white", pka = "#8fd3ff", direct = m_orange)
p5 <- ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = sachs_solid, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = kind), linewidth = 0.7, arrow = sachs_arw) +

  geom_curve(data = sachs_dashed[i, ], aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = kind), linewidth = 0.8,
             linetype = "dashed", curvature = sachs_dashed$curv[i], arrow = sachs_arw)
p5 <- p5 +
  geom_text(data = filter(sachs_nodes, name != "hat"), aes(x, y, label = name, fontface = if_else(bold, "bold", "plain")),
            colour = "white", size = 7, family = "serif") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 0.6, label = 'widehat("p44/42")', parse = TRUE, colour = "white", size = 7, family = "serif") +

bg_save(p5, "part5-sachs-ecm.png")

## Where we left off {minutes="2"}

::: {.notes}
The title slide's question first (its minutes are counted here), then this table.
:::

| Loss | Best prediction at $x$ | |
|---|---|---|
| Squared error, $(y - \hat y)^2$ | the conditional mean, $\mathbb E[Y \mid X = x]$ | optimal model theorem |
| Absolute error, $\lvert y - \hat y \rvert$ | the conditional median | stated |
| A miss costs $c_{FN}$, a false alarm $c_{FP}$ | predict $1$ when $p(x) > c^\star = \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}$ | optimal threshold theorem |

**Decision principle**: choose the prediction $\hat y$ that minimizes the expected loss given the inputs, $\mathbb E[\ell(Y, \hat y) \mid X = x]$

## {.inverse}

### Part 1: regression uncertainty and intervals

## A prediction for one person {minutes="2"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: if you are that person, what should a 90 percent interval promise you?

The competition scored averages; a deployed model answers one person at a time.
:::

So far, competitors submit models that predict, and the winning model is chosen by best score on the evaluation dataset: an average over many people

Now the winning model is deployed. A new person arrives with inputs $x_0$ and is told $\hat f(x_0)$. How far off might that be?

::: {.ask}
You are that person. What should a "90% interval" for your outcome promise you?
:::

. . .

That the interval, call it $\hat C(x_0)$, covers outcomes of people with your inputs 90% of the time: $P\big(Y \in \hat C(X) \mid X = x_0\big) \ge 0.9$, **conditional coverage**

## Two kinds of interval

::: {.notes}
lm's 90 percent confidence and prediction intervals. The confidence band shrinks with n; the prediction band does not.
:::

At a new $x_0$, $Y_0 = f^\star(x_0) + \varepsilon_0$

- **Confidence interval** for $f^\star(x_0)$ (dark): uncertainty about the fit; it narrows as $n$ grows
- **Prediction interval** for $Y_0$ (light): must also cover $\varepsilon_0$; it does not narrow below the noise

```{r}
#| label: ci-pi
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| fig-align: center
# A straight line with constant noise; lm's 90% confidence and prediction intervals at two sample sizes.
ci_pi <- function(n) {
  d <- tibble(x = runif(n, 0, 10)) |> mutate(y = 1 + 0.5 * x + rnorm(n))
  fit <- lm(y ~ x, d)
  g <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 101))
  ci <- predict(fit, g, interval = "confidence", level = 0.9)
  pr <- predict(fit, g, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)
  panel <- factor(paste0("n = ", format(n, big.mark = ",")), levels = c("n = 30", "n = 1,000"))
  list(d = mutate(d, panel = panel),
       g = mutate(g, fit = ci[, "fit"], cl = ci[, "lwr"], cu = ci[, "upr"], pl = pr[, "lwr"], pu = pr[, "upr"], panel = panel))
}
cp <- list(ci_pi(30), ci_pi(1000))
cp_g <- bind_rows(cp[[1]]$g, cp[[2]]$g); cp_d <- bind_rows(cp[[1]]$d, slice_sample(cp[[2]]$d, n = 300))
ggplot(cp_g, aes(x)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pl, ymax = pu), fill = v_teal, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = cl, ymax = cu), fill = v_dark, alpha = 0.55) + geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = v_dark) +
  geom_point(data = cp_d, aes(y = y), size = 0.8, alpha = 0.4) + facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "y") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

::: {.retrieval}
Bias--variance at $x_0$: $\sigma^2 + \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance}$; no amount of data shrinks $\sigma^2$
:::

## An interval $\hat f(x_0) \pm C$ {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: how could we compute C for each kind of interval?

For f-star(x_0): C from how much f-hat(x_0) varies between training samples (centered on f-star(x_0) only if f-hat has no bias there). For Y_0: C from how far outcomes fall from predictions.
QUESTION: which loss gives the 90th percentile? For a 90 percent interval, C is the 90th percentile of the absolute residuals; the answer is on the next two slides.
:::

The simplest interval: $\hat C(x_0) = \big[\hat f(x_0) - C,\ \hat f(x_0) + C\big]$, for a number $C$

::: {.ask}
How could we compute $C$ for each kind of interval, for $f^\star(x_0)$ and for $Y_0$?
:::

. . .

- $f^\star(x_0)$: how much $\hat f(x_0)$ varies between samples (a standard error, the bootstrap)
- $Y_0$: how far outcomes fall from predictions, a **quantile** of the absolute residuals $|y_i - \hat f(x_i)|$

. . .

::: {.ask}
Squared loss: the mean. Absolute loss: the median. Which loss: the 90th percentile?
:::

## Finding the quantile {.inverse minutes="2"}

::: {.notes}
Rush: the heuristic for the quantile; the theorem is next. Count who gains and who loses as the prediction moves up a little.
:::

Charge $\tau$ for each unit of underprediction ($y > \hat y$) and $1 - \tau$ for each unit of overprediction ($y < \hat y$). Move the prediction up from $\hat y$ to $\hat y + \delta$:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- an outcome above $\hat y$: its loss falls by $\tau\delta$
- an outcome below $\hat y$: its loss rises by $(1 - \tau)\delta$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| label: heuristic-density
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 2.0
#| dark: true
# A right-skewed density with a prediction y-hat marked: below it, the share F(y-hat); above it, 1 - F(y-hat).
a0 <- 4.2
dens <- tibble(y = seq(0, 14, length.out = 400)) |> mutate(d = dgamma(y, shape = 3, rate = 0.6))
ggplot(dens, aes(y, d)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(dens, y <= a0), fill = m_pink, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_area(data = filter(dens, y >= a0), fill = v_teal, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = a0, linewidth = 1, colour = "white") +
  annotate("text", x = a0, y = 0.255, label = "hat(y)", parse = TRUE, size = 6, hjust = -0.4, colour = "white") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.05, label = "F(hat(y))", parse = TRUE, colour = "white", size = 5.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.6, y = 0.10, label = "1 - F(hat(y))", parse = TRUE, colour = "white", size = 5.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "y", y = NULL) + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

With $F$ the distribution function of $Y$ given $X = x$, the expected change is about
$$
\delta\,\big[(1 - \tau)F(\hat y) - \tau\,(1 - F(\hat y))\big] = \delta\,\big[F(\hat y) - \tau\big]
$$

Keep moving up while $F(\hat y) < \tau$; stop where $F(\hat y) = \tau$: the **$\tau$-quantile**. For the 90th percentile, $\tau = 0.9$

## Quantile optimality

::: {.notes}
Stated; the proof is a pre-seminar exercise. The finite mean keeps the expected loss finite.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
**Pinball loss**:
$$
\rho_\tau(y - \hat y) = (y - \hat y)\,\big(\tau - \mathbf 1\{y < \hat y\}\big)
$$
$\tau\,(y - \hat y)$ for an underprediction, $(1 - \tau)(\hat y - y)$ for an overprediction. With $\tau = \frac12$, half the absolute error
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{r}
#| label: pinball-plot
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 2.7
expand_grid(u = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 201), tau = c(0.5, 0.9)) |>
  mutate(loss = pin(u, tau)) |>
  ggplot(aes(u, loss, colour = factor(tau))) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`0.5` = v_dark, `0.9` = v_teal), name = expression(tau)) +
  labs(x = expression(y - hat(y)), y = "loss")
```
:::
:::

::: {.leave}
**Quantile optimality theorem.** If $Y \mid X = x$ has a continuous distribution with a finite mean and $0 < \tau < 1$, then the conditional $\tau$-quantile $q_\tau(x)$ minimizes $\mathbb E[\rho_\tau(Y - \hat y) \mid X = x]$ over $\hat y$ (uniquely, unless the distribution function is flat at $\tau$)
:::

Squared loss gave the mean; half the absolute error, $\tau = \frac12$, gives the median

## Quantile regression

::: {.notes}
rq() solves it as a linear program. Dashed: the true quantiles. The lines fan out with the noise and miss the curvature.
:::

Minimize the average pinball loss over a class: $\hat q_\tau = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} \frac1n \sum_i \rho_\tau\big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)$. Here $\mathcal F$ is linear; 1,000 simulated points: noise that grows with $x$, a bump at 3, few points with $x$ between 4 and 6

```{r}
#| label: qr-linear-show
#| echo: true
fit_qr <- rq(y ~ x, tau = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), data = het_train)
```

```{r}
#| label: qr-linear-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-align: center
taus <- c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)
true_q <- map_dfr(taus, function(t) mutate(x_grid, tau = t, q = f_sim(x) + s_sim(x) * qnorm(t)))
lin_q <- map_dfr(seq_along(taus), function(k) mutate(x_grid, tau = taus[k], q = predict(fit_qr, x_grid)[, k]))
q_cols <- c(`0.05` = m_pink, `0.5` = v_dark, `0.95` = v_teal)
ggplot(het_train, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = true_q, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = lin_q, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = q_cols, name = expression(tau)) + labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

## The same loss, a flexible model

::: {.notes}
xgboost's reg:quantileerror optimizes a smooth approximation to the pinball loss. Depth 2, rate 0.05, 300 iterations, leaves of at least 30; not tuned.
:::

Boosted trees with the pinball loss: each tree is built from the negative gradient $\tau - \mathbf 1\{y_i < \hat f(x_i)\}$, which pushes the fit up where points lie above it

```{r}
#| label: qr-boost-show
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
xgboost(x, y, objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = 0.95, max_depth = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: qr-boost-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.75
#| fig-align: center
# The code shown above, for each tau, with the rest of the settings.
boost_q <- function(tau) xgboost(x = as.matrix(het_train["x"]), y = het_train$y,
  objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = tau,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
fit_bq <- map(taus, boost_q)
boost_curve <- map_dfr(seq_along(taus), function(k) mutate(x_grid, tau = taus[k], q = predict(fit_bq[[k]], as.matrix(x_grid))))
ggplot(het_train, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = true_q, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = boost_curve, aes(y = q, colour = factor(tau)), linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = q_cols, name = expression(tau)) + labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

::: {.retrieval}
Boosting: each small tree approximates the negative gradient of the training loss
:::

## Challenges with local intervals

::: {.notes}
Linear model, constant noise: lm's prediction interval (widens slightly at the ends: the fitted mean's uncertainty). Mean and variance: |residuals| regressed on x, times sqrt(pi/2) and 1.645. Dashed: the true 5 and 95 percent quantiles.
x between 4 and 6: `r sum(het_train$x >= 4 & het_train$x < 6)` of the 1,000 points, so about 3 beyond each true quantile.
:::

A **local** interval's edges change with $x$: $\hat C(x) = [\hat q_{0.05}(x), \hat q_{0.95}(x)]$, two quantile fits

```{r}
#| label: three-intervals
#| include: false
z90 <- qnorm(0.95)
fit_lm <- lm(y ~ x, het_train)
fit_abs <- lm(abs(resid(fit_lm)) ~ x, het_train)
interval_fns <- list(
  `linear model, constant noise` = function(d) { p <- predict(fit_lm, d, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9); cbind(p[, "lwr"], p[, "upr"]) },
  `mean and variance` = function(d) { m <- predict(fit_lm, d); s <- predict(fit_abs, d) * sqrt(pi / 2); cbind(m - z90 * s, m + z90 * s) },
  `linear quantiles` = function(d) predict(fit_qr, d)[, c(1, 3)],
  `boosted quantiles` = function(d) cbind(predict(fit_bq[[1]], as.matrix(d["x"])), predict(fit_bq[[3]], as.matrix(d["x"])))
)
bands <- imap_dfr(interval_fns, function(fn, nm) { b <- fn(x_grid); tibble(x = x_grid$x, lo = b[, 1], hi = b[, 2], method = nm) }) |>
  mutate(method = fct_inorder(method))
true_band <- x_grid |> mutate(lo = f_sim(x) - z90 * s_sim(x), hi = f_sim(x) + z90 * s_sim(x))
```

```{r}
#| label: three-intervals-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(filter(bands, method != "linear quantiles"), aes(x)) +
  geom_point(data = het_train, aes(y = y), alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = v_teal, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = true_band, aes(y = lo), linetype = "dashed") + geom_line(data = true_band, aes(y = hi), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ method) + labs(x = "x (dashed: the true 5% and 95% quantiles)", y = "y") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

- Edges near $x$ come from rows near $x$: few in 4 to 6; at 3 the quantiles change fast
- Extreme quantiles are harder to learn than the mean: 1 row in 20 lies beyond each edge
- Rigid models (left, middle) use every row at every $x$: stable, wrong where they misfit

## Checking an interval {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: we claim 90 percent intervals; how do you check, and what could the check miss?
:::

::: {.ask}
We claim 90 percent intervals. With fresh data in hand, how do you check the claim, and what could the check miss?
:::

## Checking an interval on fresh data

```{r}
#| label: coverage
#| include: false
cov_methods <- c("linear model, constant noise", "mean and variance", "boosted quantiles")
cov_pts <- imap_dfr(interval_fns[cov_methods], function(fn, nm) {
  b <- fn(het_fresh)
  tibble(method = nm, x = het_fresh$x, y = het_fresh$y, lo = b[, 1], hi = b[, 2],
         inside = het_fresh$y >= b[, 1] & het_fresh$y <= b[, 2], width = b[, 2] - b[, 1])
}) |> mutate(method = factor(method, levels = cov_methods))
cov_all <- cov_pts |> group_by(method) |> summarise(all = mean(inside), width = mean(width))
# Five ranges of x; a range is flagged when its coverage, as shown (a whole percent), is more than 3 points
# from 90: two binomial standard errors for the about 400 fresh points with x between 4 and 6, more elsewhere.
cov_rng <- cov_pts |> mutate(mid = 2 * floor(pmin(x, 9.999) / 2) + 1) |>
  group_by(method, mid) |> summarise(cov = mean(inside), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
flag_off <- function(cov) abs(round(100 * cov) - 90) > 3
cov_rng <- cov_rng |> mutate(off = flag_off(cov))
pct <- function(v) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v)
pct1 <- function(v) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * v)
# Fresh points inside (grey) and outside (pink) each interval, with the coverage of each range of x on top.
# One point in `every` is drawn and the interval is tinted over the points (and outlined, where its edges are
# smooth), so that it shows; the coverage rates are those of all the points.
coverage_plot <- function(pts, rng, curve = NULL, outline = TRUE, every = 3, legend = "right") {
  y_lab <- max(pts$y) + 2
  band <- arrange(pts, method, x)
  ggplot(pts |> group_by(method) |> filter(row_number() %% every == 1) |> ungroup(), aes(x, y)) +
    geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
    geom_point(aes(colour = inside), size = 0.9, alpha = 0.75) +
    geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = v_dark, alpha = 0.12) +
    { if (outline) geom_line(data = band, aes(y = lo), colour = v_dark, linewidth = 0.4) } +
    { if (outline) geom_line(data = band, aes(y = hi), colour = v_dark, linewidth = 0.4) } +
    { if (!is.null(curve)) geom_line(data = curve, aes(x, y), linetype = "dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE) } +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(2, 4, 6, 8), colour = "grey70", linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_text(data = rng, aes(x = mid, y = y_lab, label = pct(cov), fontface = if_else(off, "bold", "plain")),
              colour = if_else(rng$off, m_pink, "grey30"), size = 4.6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~ method) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey45", `FALSE` = m_pink), labels = c(`TRUE` = "inside", `FALSE` = "outside"), name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) + coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(x = "x", y = "fresh y") +
    theme(legend.position = legend, strip.text = element_text(size = 15), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
```

::: {.notes}
`r format(nrow(het_fresh), big.mark = ",")` fresh points, every tenth drawn. Above each panel: coverage by range (`r sum(het_fresh$x >= 4 & het_fresh$x < 6)` points for x between 4 and 6, about `r format(round(sum(het_fresh$x < 4) / 200) * 100, big.mark = ",")` in the others); pink when more than 3 points from 90.
Mean widths `r sprintf("%.1f", cov_all$width[1])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", cov_all$width[2])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", cov_all$width[3])`; true quantiles `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(2 * z90 * s_sim(het_fresh$x)))`.
:::

```{r}
#| label: coverage-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center
coverage_plot(cov_pts, cov_rng, every = 10)
```

Top: coverage in each range of $x$, pink if more than 3 points from 90%. Overall: `r pct(cov_all$all[1])`, `r pct(cov_all$all[2])`, `r pct(cov_all$all[3])`. Widening never lowers coverage: check width too

## Bias, variance and intervals

```{r}
#| label: bias-variance
#| include: false
# The data of the previous slides: the 1,000 training rows to fit, 1,000 more to tune, 1,000 held out; checked on the
# fresh rows. The interval: f-hat(x) plus or minus C. On this slide C is the 90th percentile of the absolute residuals
# on the training rows; on the next (split conformal), the ceiling(0.9 * 1001)-th smallest absolute residual on 1,000
# rows not used to fit.
het_tune <- sim(1000); het_hold <- sim(1000)
fit_line <- lm(y ~ x, het_train)
fit_rf1 <- randomForest(y ~ x, data = het_train, ntree = 300)
C_train <- function(fit) quantile(abs(het_train$y - predict(fit, het_train)), 0.9)
C_from <- function(fit, d) sort(abs(d$y - predict(fit, d)))[ceiling(0.9 * (nrow(d) + 1))]
# Fresh points inside and outside each interval, overall coverage and width, and coverage by range of x.
bv_cover <- function(models) {
  pts <- imap_dfr(models, function(m, nm) {
    p <- predict(m[[1]], het_fresh)
    tibble(method = nm, x = het_fresh$x, y = het_fresh$y, lo = p - m[[2]], hi = p + m[[2]], inside = abs(het_fresh$y - p) <= m[[2]])
  }) |> mutate(method = fct_inorder(method))
  list(pts = pts, all = pts |> group_by(method) |> summarise(all = mean(inside), width = mean(hi - lo)),
       rng = pts |> mutate(mid = 2 * floor(pmin(x, 9.999) / 2) + 1) |> group_by(method, mid) |>
         summarise(cov = mean(inside), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(off = flag_off(cov)))
}
bv <- bv_cover(list(`a line` = list(fit_line, C_train(fit_line)), `a random forest` = list(fit_rf1, C_train(fit_rf1))))
```

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: how could we choose C so that the forest's interval covers 90 percent of new outcomes?

The data of the previous slides, every tenth fresh point drawn. Dashed: the curve. Line: `r pct(bv$all$all[1])` overall: its residuals include its bias and the noise at every x, so the level is about right on average and wrong by range.
Forest with randomForest's defaults (nodes down to 5 rows): `r pct(bv$all$all[2])` overall, `r sprintf("%.1f", bv$all$width[2])` wide.
:::

$\hat f(x) \pm C$, with $C$ the 90th percentile of the absolute residuals on the **training** rows

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
```{r}
#| label: bias-variance-plot
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 3.3
coverage_plot(bv$pts, bv$rng, curve = mutate(x_grid, y = f_sim(x)), outline = FALSE, every = 10, legend = "none")
```
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
- **Bias**: the line misses the bends
- **Variance**: the forest follows the noise in its own rows; residuals there are too small
- **One $C$** for every $x$, though the noise grows
:::
:::

::: {.ask}
How could we choose $C$ so that the forest's interval covers 90% of new outcomes?
:::

## Residuals from held-out rows {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: held-out
#| include: false
# The forest's node size chosen on the tuning rows (smallest MSE there); then C from the held-out rows, or from the
# tuning rows themselves.
sizes <- c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320)
rf_sizes <- map(sizes, function(s) randomForest(y ~ x, data = het_train, ntree = 300, nodesize = s))
size_mse <- map_dbl(rf_sizes, function(f) mse(het_tune$y, predict(f, het_tune)))
fit_rf_tuned <- rf_sizes[[which.min(size_mse)]]
ho <- bv_cover(list(`C from 1,000 held-out rows` = list(fit_rf_tuned, C_from(fit_rf_tuned, het_hold)),
                    `C from the 1,000 tuning rows` = list(fit_rf_tuned, C_from(fit_rf_tuned, het_tune))))
ho_default <- bv_cover(list(d = list(fit_rf1, C_from(fit_rf1, het_hold))))$all
ho_train <- mean(abs(het_fresh$y - predict(fit_rf_tuned, het_fresh)) <= C_train(fit_rf_tuned))
```

::: {.notes}
Node size `r sizes[which.min(size_mse)]`, the best of 5 to 320 on the tuning rows. Widths `r sprintf("%.1f", ho$all$width[1])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", ho$all$width[2])`. The default forest with held-out C: `r pct(ho_default$all)`, `r sprintf("%.1f", ho_default$width)` wide. The tuned forest with its own training residuals: `r pct(ho_train)`.
Why 1,001: the new row's residual is equally likely to take any rank among the 1,001. Coverage varies by about 0.9 points (sd) from one held-out set of 1,000 to another.
Tuning rows: with a handful of settings tried the optimism is small. In 150 repeats outside the deck (constant noise, sets of 500 rows, six settings): 90.1 and 90.0 percent, within simulation noise.
By range: one C for every x while the noise grows; the next slide.
:::

The forest again, its node size now tuned on 1,000 **tuning** rows

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
```{r}
#| label: held-out-plot
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 3.3
coverage_plot(ho$pts, ho$rng, curve = mutate(x_grid, y = f_sim(x)), outline = FALSE, every = 10, legend = "none")
```
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
**Split conformal** (Lei et al. 2018): $C$ from 1,000 rows not used to fit, their 901st smallest absolute residual, $\lceil 0.9 \times 1001 \rceil$

Overall `r pct(ho$all$all[1])` and `r pct(ho$all$all[2])`, but not in every range
:::
:::

The tuning rows chose the node size, so residuals on them may be slightly optimistic

::: {.retrieval}
Optimism theorem: training error underestimates the risk
:::

## Coverage on average, and at every $x$

```{r}
#| label: grow
#| include: false
# Coverage at each x, computed exactly: the noise is normal with known mean and sd, so for an interval [lo, hi] at x,
# P(Y in [lo, hi] | X = x) = pnorm((hi - f(x)) / s(x)) - pnorm((lo - f(x)) / s(x)). Averaged over fits on fresh
# training rows: conditional coverage with the training rows random too. Two intervals: f-hat(x) plus or minus C
# (boosted trees for the mean on n rows, C from n held-out rows; 5 fits), and two boosted quantile fits on n rows
# (30 fits).
bst <- function(d, objective, ...) xgboost(x = as.matrix(d["x"]), y = d$y, objective = objective, ...,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
grow_x <- tibble(x = seq(0.005, 9.995, by = 0.01)); grow_gx <- as.matrix(grow_x)
cov_at <- function(lo, hi) pnorm((hi - f_sim(grow_x$x)) / s_sim(grow_x$x)) - pnorm((lo - f_sim(grow_x$x)) / s_sim(grow_x$x))
grow <- map_dfr(c(1000, 8000, 32000), function(n) map_dfr(1:30, function(r) {
  d <- sim(n)
  out <- tibble(method = "two quantile fits", n = n, x = grow_x$x,
                cov = cov_at(predict(bst(d, "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = 0.05), grow_gx),
                             predict(bst(d, "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = 0.95), grow_gx)))
  if (r <= 5) {
    h <- sim(n); m <- bst(d, "reg:squarederror"); C <- sort(abs(h$y - predict(m, as.matrix(h["x"]))))[ceiling(0.9 * (n + 1))]
    p <- predict(m, grow_gx)
    out <- bind_rows(out, tibble(method = "one C for every x", n = n, x = grow_x$x, cov = cov_at(p - C, p + C)))
  }
  out
})) |> group_by(method, n, x) |> summarise(cov = mean(cov), .groups = "drop")
grow_range <- function(m, n0) with(filter(grow, method == m, n == n0), range(round(100 * cov)))
grow_plot <- function(m) ggplot(filter(grow, method == m), aes(x, cov, colour = factor(n))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4, xmax = 6, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.9, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`1000` = m_pink, `8000` = v_teal, `32000` = v_dark), labels = c("1,000", "8,000", "32,000"), name = "n") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.65, 1)) +
  labs(x = "x (shaded: few rows)", y = "coverage at x", title = m) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(size = 16), legend.text = element_text(size = 13),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 14))
```

::: {.notes}
Lei et al. (2018), section 2.2: for any model; also at most 0.9 + 1/(m + 1) with m held-out rows, when the residuals are continuous. The probability averages over the held-out rows too.
Plot: coverage at each x, exact from the known noise; boosted trees for the mean on n rows, C from n more; averaged over 5 fits. As n grows the interval tends to the curve plus or minus one number, the 90th percentile of |noise| over all x.
:::

::: {.leave}
**Conformal coverage theorem** (split conformal: Lei et al. 2018). If the rows are independent draws from one distribution, then for any model $P\big(Y \in \hat C(X)\big) \ge 0.9$, on average over $X$: **marginal coverage**
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
**Conditional coverage**: $P\big(Y \in \hat C(X) \mid X = x\big) \ge 0.9$ at every $x$, what the one person wanted

One $C$ for every $x$, and noise that grows with $x$: too wide where the noise is small, too narrow where it is large, whatever $n$
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{r}
#| label: grow-one-c
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: 90%
grow_plot("one C for every x")
```
:::
:::

## Coverage at every $x$, as $n$ grows

::: {.notes}
Exact coverage at each x from the known noise, averaged over 30 fits for each n: conditional coverage with the training rows random too, as in the impossibility theorem. No held-out rows, so the fits under-cover a little at small n (conformalized quantile regression, after the conclusion, corrects the average). At n = 32,000 the curve stays between `r grow_range("two quantile fits", 32000)[1]` and `r grow_range("two quantile fits", 32000)[2]` percent.
Near 0 the curve is steep (slope 3) and the noise smallest (sd 0.5): the quantiles change fast relative to the noise. The bump at 3: height 3, sd 0.2.
Formal version, for conformalized quantile fits: Sesia and Candès (2020), Theorem 1 and its corollary. Consistency there: the fits' mean squared error at a new X tends to zero.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{r}
#| label: grow-quantiles
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| out-width: 100%
grow_plot("two quantile fits")
```
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
Edges fitted near each $x$: two quantile fits on $n$ rows. The noise is known, so coverage at each $x$ can be computed exactly; here averaged over 30 fits

- At $n$ = 1,000 it dips where the quantiles change fast relative to the noise (near 0, at the bump) and where the rows are few (4 to 6)
- The dips fill in as $n$ grows, **if** the fits approach the true quantiles (**consistency**)
:::
:::

## Coverage at every $x$ in many dimensions

::: {.notes}
Variance: the interval between the 5th and 95th percentiles of n rows drawn at x covers a share of the distribution with a Beta distribution, mean about 0.9, variance about 0.9 x 0.1 / n. One edge alone: tau(1 - tau) / n = 0.0475 / n; the two edges' errors are correlated (covariance 0.05 x 0.05 / n), so (0.0475 + 0.0475 - 2 x 0.0025) / n = 0.09 / n. Bias: a normal outcome, both edges half a standard deviation too high.
So the speed depends on the rows near x, on how fast the quantiles change with x compared with the noise, and on the number of inputs. Table: five bins per input, 2,000 rows spread evenly. A smoother, a tree or boosting instead of bins: the same trade-off, since a neighborhood holding enough rows is wide.
The variance is that of a share of 0.9 among n_x rows.
:::

An interval at $x$ is learned from the $n_x$ rows near $x$. Its coverage there misses 90% by

- **Variance**: about $\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1 / n_x}$: 4 points with 50 rows, 1.3 with 500
- **Bias**: rows farther from $x$ have different quantiles. Edges off by half a noise standard deviation: `r round(100 * (pnorm(qnorm(0.95) + 0.5) - pnorm(0.5 - qnorm(0.95))))`%, not 90%

More inputs, fewer rows near $x$. 2,000 rows, 5 bins for each input:

| Inputs | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Rows per bin, $n_x$ | 400 | 80 | 16 | 0.6 |
| $\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1 / n_x}$, points | 1.5 | 3.4 | 7.5 | -- |

::: {.retrieval}
Curse of dimensionality: in ten dimensions, a cube holding 10% of the population spans 79% of each axis
:::

## Conditional coverage without assumptions

::: {.notes}
Stated (Barber et al., Proposition 2.2). Their wording: at every x that is not an atom of the inputs' distribution; "continuous inputs" is the slide's simplification (last slide before the references).
Infinite expected length: an interval that is safe at every x for every distribution is useless.
:::

Fits that approach the true quantiles, enough rows near $x$, quantiles that change slowly: each is an assumption about the distribution. With none:

::: {.leave}
**Impossibility of distribution-free conditional coverage.** If a procedure covers with probability at least $1 - \alpha$ given $X = x$, in finite samples, for every distribution and almost every $x$, then wherever the inputs are continuous its intervals have infinite expected length (Barber et al. 2021). Guarantees for groups (each range of $x$, say), and results under assumptions or as $n$ grows, remain possible
:::

::: {.retrieval}
No free lunch theorem: no method does best on every distribution; a guarantee at every $x$ needs an assumption about the distribution
:::

## Ways to make an interval {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: each method assumes something and claims a kind of coverage; the note on the course page has this table and how each works. CQR: the slide after the conclusion.
Exchangeable: the rows' joint distribution does not change when they are reordered; independent draws from one distribution are exchangeable (the second slide after the conclusion).
:::

| Method | Assumes | Can claim |
|---|---|---|
| Linear model, normal noise | linear mean, constant variance | 90% at every $x$, if right |
| Mean and variance models | both right, normal noise | about 90% at every $x$, if right |
| Quantile regression | the quantile model right | 90% at every $x$ as $n$ grows, if right |
| Split conformal (Lei et al. 2018) | exchangeable rows | at least 90% marginally; one width |
| CQR (Romano et al. 2019) | exchangeable rows | at least 90% marginally; widths from the fits; at every $x$ as $n$ grows, if the fits are consistent |

More in the note on the course page, "Prediction intervals and calibration"; CQR is also on the slide after the conclusion

## {.inverse .center background-image="img/part3-logistic.png" background-size="cover" background-opacity="0.5" background-color="#440154"}

::: {.notes}
Compress: a probability is calibrated when it matches a frequency; check it on fresh data; recalibrate on rows not used to fit; check it within groups.
:::

### Part 2: classification uncertainty and calibration

## Data: NHANES

::: {.notes}
NHANESraw in the R package NHANES; the data note is on the course page. Adults of 20 and over with every column used here recorded.
The survey samples some groups at higher rates on purpose, and we do not use its weights. Diabetes: ever told by a doctor or health professional, so undiagnosed diabetes counts as no.
:::

The US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2009 to 2012 (R package `NHANES`): interviews and physical examinations. We use `r format(nrow(nh), big.mark = ",")` adults aged 20 and over

| | |
|----|------------------------|
| Outcomes | **diabetes**, as told by a doctor (`r round(100 * mean(nh$diabetes))`% yes); later, **systolic blood pressure** (mm Hg) |
| Measurements | age, gender, weight, height, BMI, pulse, total and HDL cholesterol, family income relative to the poverty line, physically active or not |
| Groups | race and ethnicity, in the survey's five groups |
| Split | at random: 4,000 training adults; 3,000 tuning adults; `r format(nrow(nh_test), big.mark = ",")` test adults, used once |

- Not a sample of the US population: the survey samples some groups at higher rates, and we do not use its weights

## Calibration {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: a model gives p-hat = 0.2 to 500 adults; what should be true of them?

About 100 should have diabetes. Calibration conditions on the score's value, not on x.
:::

::: {.ask}
A model gives $\hat p = 0.2$ to 500 adults: their probability of having diabetes. What should be true of them?
:::

. . .

About 100 of them should have diabetes. A score $\hat p$ is **calibrated** if
$$
P\big(Y = 1 \mid \hat p(X)\big) = \hat p(X)
$$

The same idea as coverage: a stated probability should match a frequency. It conditions on the score, not on $x$

## Calibration and decisions {minutes="3"}

::: {.notes}
Calibrated: P(Y = 1 | p-hat) = p-hat, so the optimal threshold theorem applies with the score as the only input: optimal among rules based on the score, not necessarily among rules using all of x.
If asked: p-hat = 0.25 + 0.5 p is miscalibrated but gives the right decisions at 0.5.
:::

A probability is acted on: a risk told to a patient, a premium set from an expected cost, a threshold set from the costs of errors

- The optimal threshold theorem cuts the true $p(x)$ at $c^\star$; we have only $\hat p$. If $\hat p$ is calibrated, cutting it at $c^\star$ is optimal among rules based on that score
- If not, $c^\star$ can pick the wrong people. At $c^\star = 0.25$, adults given $\hat p = 0.2$, of whom 40% have diabetes, are not referred for a test, although referring them costs less on average
- Calibration is not accuracy. The base rate, $`r sprintf("%.2f", mean(nh_train$diabetes))`$ for every adult, is calibrated and separates no one. An increasing transformation keeps a score's ranking (and AUC), not its calibration

::: {.retrieval}
Optimal threshold theorem: with costs $c_{FP}$ and $c_{FN}$, the rule that minimizes expected cost at $x$ predicts $1$ exactly when $p(x) > c^\star = c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$
:::

## Reliability diagram

```{r}
#| label: calibration-fits
#| include: false
cal_inputs <- c("Age", "male", "BMI", "Pulse", "BPSysAve", "TotChol", "DirectChol", "Poverty", "active")
fit_lr <- glm(diabetes ~ Age + male + BMI + Pulse + BPSysAve + TotChol + DirectChol + Poverty + active,
              family = binomial, data = nh_train)
fit_xg <- xgboost(x = as.matrix(nh_train[cal_inputs]), y = factor(nh_train$diabetes), nthread = 1)   # defaults: depth 6, rate 0.3, 100 iterations
p_lr <- predict(fit_lr, nh_tune, type = "response")
p_xg <- predict(fit_xg, as.matrix(nh_tune[cal_inputs]))
p_xg_train <- predict(fit_xg, as.matrix(nh_train[cal_inputs]))
p_lr_train <- fitted(fit_lr)
y_tune <- nh_tune$diabetes
# Bins with equal numbers of adults, by the score's value.
reliability <- function(p, y, bins = 10) tibble(p, y) |>
  mutate(bin = ntile(p, bins)) |>
  group_by(bin) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_p = mean(p), freq = mean(y), .groups = "drop")
base_rate <- mean(nh_train$diabetes)
rel_all <- bind_rows(
  reliability(p_lr_train, nh_train$diabetes) |> mutate(score = "logistic regression", rows = "training adults"),
  reliability(p_xg_train, nh_train$diabetes) |> mutate(score = "boosted trees", rows = "training adults"),
  reliability(p_lr, y_tune) |> mutate(score = "logistic regression", rows = "tuning adults"),
  reliability(p_xg, y_tune) |> mutate(score = "boosted trees", rows = "tuning adults")) |>
  mutate(score = fct_inorder(score))
rel_plot_of <- function(d) ggplot(d, aes(mean_p, freq, colour = rows)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.6) + facet_wrap(~ score) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`tuning adults` = v_dark, `training adults` = "grey55"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = c("0", "0.5", "1")) + coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "predicted probability (bin average)", y = "share with diabetes") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16), legend.position = "right")
rel_top_of <- function(r) filter(rel_all, score == "boosted trees", rows == r) |> slice_max(mean_p)
```

::: {.notes}
Diabetes as reported; nine inputs, race and ethnicity left out. xgboost defaults (depth 6, 100 iterations). Ten bins with equal numbers of adults.
Boosted trees, top bin on the training adults: `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * rel_top_of("training adults")$mean_p)` percent predicted, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * rel_top_of("training adults")$freq)` percent with diabetes. Logistic regression: its fitted probabilities sum to the number of cases on its own rows.
:::

Adults in ten bins by score: each bin's share with diabetes against its average score. Two scores from nine measurements, on the 4,000 **training** adults used to fit them

```{r}
#| label: reliability-train-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-align: center
rel_plot_of(filter(rel_all, rows == "training adults"))
```

On the diagonal: calibrated. On their own adults, logistic regression is; the boosted trees look too cautious at the top

## Reliability on fresh adults

::: {.notes}
Read one point first: the ringed one, described in the legend. Boosted trees: too cautious at the top on their own adults, too confident on fresh ones.
:::

The same two scores on 3,000 **tuning** adults, who played no part in fitting them

```{r}
#| label: reliability-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
# The top bin of the boosted score on the tuning adults: ringed, and described in the legend.
rel_top <- rel_top_of("tuning adults") |>
  mutate(text = sprintf("ringed: %d adults,\n%.0f%% predicted,\n%.0f%% with diabetes", n, 100 * mean_p, 100 * freq))
rel_plot_of(rel_all) +
  geom_point(data = rel_top, aes(mean_p, freq, shape = text), size = 6.5, stroke = 1.3, colour = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = 1, name = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1), shape = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
  theme(legend.key.height = unit(1.6, "lines"))
```

Logistic regression (10 coefficients) hardly moves. Boosted trees (100 trees): too confident at the top, the opposite of what their training adults said

## Recalibration

::: {.notes}
Fitted on 1,500 tuning adults, checked on the other 1,500; five bins of 300. An increasing map keeps the ranking, so the AUC is unchanged.
:::

```{r}
#| label: recalibration
#| include: false
half_a <- 1:1500; half_b <- 1501:3000
logit_p <- function(p) qlogis(pmin(pmax(p, 1e-4), 1 - 1e-4))
recal <- glm(y ~ s, family = binomial, data = tibble(y = y_tune[half_a], s = logit_p(p_xg[half_a])))
p_recal <- predict(recal, tibble(s = logit_p(p_xg[half_b])), type = "response")
b_recal <- coef(recal)[["s"]]
logloss <- function(p, y) -mean(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
```

A map from the old score to a new one, learned on half the tuning adults, checked on the other half: a logistic regression of the label on $\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p$, giving $\mathrm{logit}\,\tilde p = a + b\,\mathrm{logit}\,\hat p$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: recalibration-plot
#| fig-width: 6.0
#| fig-height: 3.6
recal_map <- tibble(p = seq(0.005, 0.995, length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(p_new = predict(recal, tibble(s = logit_p(p)), type = "response"))
map_plot <- ggplot(recal_map, aes(p, p_new)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3, colour = v_dark) +
  geom_rug(data = tibble(p = p_xg[half_b]), aes(x = p), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.15, length = unit(0.04, "npc")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "boosted score", y = "recalibrated", title = "the map")
rel_plot <- bind_rows(reliability(p_xg[half_b], y_tune[half_b], 5) |> mutate(score = "boosted"),
                      reliability(p_recal, y_tune[half_b], 5) |> mutate(score = "recalibrated")) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_p, freq, colour = score)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(boosted = "grey55", recalibrated = v_dark), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "predicted probability", y = "share with diabetes", title = "on the other half") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
(map_plot | rel_plot) & theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
For $b > 0$ the map is increasing: the same ranking, new probabilities. $b = `r sprintf("%.2f", b_recal)`$: two adults whose boosted log-odds differ by 1 differ by `r sprintf("%.2f", b_recal)` after. Log loss on the other half: `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_xg[half_b], y_tune[half_b]))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_recal, y_tune[half_b]))`
:::
:::

## Calibration within groups {minutes="1"}

```{r}
#| label: multicalibration
#| include: false
# The logistic score of the reliability diagram (race and ethnicity left out), by the survey's five groups.
groups_of <- function(d) c(list(everyone = rep(TRUE, nrow(d))),
                           setNames(lapply(levels(d$Race1), function(l) d$Race1 == l), levels(d$Race1)))
by_group <- function(d, p) imap_dfr(groups_of(d), function(g, nm) tibble(
  group = nm, n = sum(g), observed = mean(d$diabetes[g]), predicted = mean(p[g]))) |>
  mutate(se = sqrt(observed * (1 - observed) / n))
grp <- by_group(nh_tune, p_lr) |> mutate(group = fct_inorder(group))
gap_se <- function(g) with(grp[grp$group == g, ], abs(predicted - observed) / se)
```

::: {.notes}
Bars: two standard errors. Clear gap only for White adults (`r sprintf("%.1f", gap_se("White"))` SE); Black `r sprintf("%.1f", gap_se("Black"))`, Mexican American `r sprintf("%.1f", gap_se("Mexican"))`, the rest under 2. Everyone: `r sprintf("%.1f", gap_se("everyone"))`.
:::

One score for everyone: the logistic score, with race and ethnicity left out of its inputs. Is it calibrated within each group?

```{r}
#| label: multicalibration-plot
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: 62%
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(grp, aes(y = fct_rev(group))) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = observed - 2 * se, xmax = observed + 2 * se), width = 0.25, orientation = "y", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(x = observed, colour = "share with diabetes"), size = 3.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = predicted, colour = "average score"), shape = 17, size = 3.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`share with diabetes` = "black", `average score` = m_pink), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "the logistic score, 3,000 tuning adults", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

White adults: average score `r pct1(grp$predicted[grp$group == "White"])`, `r pct1(grp$observed[grp$group == "White"])` with diabetes, a gap of `r sprintf("%.1f", gap_se("White"))` standard errors; the other gaps are about 2 standard errors or less

## Calibration and fairness

::: {.notes}
Kleinberg et al.: calibration within groups, balance for the positive class and for the negative class hold together only with perfect prediction or equal base rates. For a threshold rule, Chouldechova (2017): with different base rates, equal positive predictive value rules out equal false positive and false negative rates.
:::

- A score that is too high for one group and too low for another, cut at one threshold, refers the first group for tests more often, and the second less often, than their risk warrants
- The score **discriminates**, even with race and ethnicity left out of its inputs
- Calibration within groups is one fairness criterion among several, and they conflict: with different base rates, no imperfect score is calibrated within groups and also averages the same in each group among adults with diabetes, and among those without (Kleinberg et al. 2017)

## Multicalibration {.inverse}

```{r}
#| label: multicalibration-fix
#| include: false
# Multicalibration, in the spirit of Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018), section 3.2: for each group and each tenth of
# the score's range with at least 100 adults, if the share with diabetes and the average score differ by more
# than the tolerance, shift the scores there by the difference; repeat until none does.
multicalibrate <- function(p, y, groups, tol = 0.02, min_n = 100, max_rounds = 200) {
  shifts <- list()
  for (r in seq_len(max_rounds)) {
    moved <- FALSE
    for (g in names(groups)) for (v in 0:9) {
      cell <- groups[[g]] & pmin(floor(10 * p), 9) == v
      if (sum(cell) < min_n) next
      gap <- mean(y[cell]) - mean(p[cell])
      if (abs(gap) > tol) { p[cell] <- pmin(pmax(p[cell] + gap, 0.001), 0.999); moved <- TRUE
        shifts[[length(shifts) + 1]] <- list(g = g, v = v, gap = gap) }
    }
    if (!moved) break
  }
  list(p = p, shifts = shifts)
}
# The shifts found on the tuning adults, applied in the same order to the test adults.
apply_shifts <- function(p, groups, shifts) {
  for (s in shifts) { cell <- groups[[s$g]] & pmin(floor(10 * p), 9) == s$v; p[cell] <- pmin(pmax(p[cell] + s$gap, 0.001), 0.999) }
  p
}
mcal <- multicalibrate(p_lr, nh_tune$diabetes, groups_of(nh_tune))
p_lr_test <- predict(fit_lr, nh_test, type = "response")
p_mc_test <- apply_shifts(p_lr_test, groups_of(nh_test), mcal$shifts)
mc_test <- by_group(nh_test, p_lr_test) |>
  mutate(after = by_group(nh_test, p_mc_test)$predicted, group = fct_inorder(group),
         gap_before = abs(predicted - observed) / se, gap_after = abs(after - observed) / se)
gap_t <- function(g, when) sprintf("%.1f", mc_test[[paste0("gap_", when)]][mc_test$group == g])
```

::: {.notes}
Compress: the method in one sentence, then the result: it fixes the gap the data can establish, and only that.
Hébert-Johnson et al. (2018), definition 2.6 and section 3.2 of the arXiv version. Here: cells of at least 100 adults, shifted by the gap between the share with diabetes and the average score when it is over 0.02; `r length(mcal$shifts)` shifts, learned on the tuning adults; checked on the `r format(nrow(nh_test), big.mark = ",")` test adults, opened once.
The White gap before is `r gap_t("White", "before")` SE on the test adults, `r sprintf("%.1f", gap_se("White"))` on the tuning adults. Black: `r gap_t("Black", "before")` to `r gap_t("Black", "after")`. Log loss `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_lr_test, nh_test$diabetes))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", logloss(p_mc_test, nh_test$diabetes))`: small cells fit noise. The shifts need each adult's group.
:::

**Multicalibration** (Hébert-Johnson et al. 2018): calibrated in every group named in advance, at every range of scores. In each group and tenth of the scores, shift the scores by the gap; repeat

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
Learned on the tuning adults, checked on the test adults. Gap in standard errors:

- White (`r format(mc_test$n[mc_test$group == "White"], big.mark = ",")` adults): `r gap_t("White", "before")` to `r gap_t("White", "after")`
- Mexican American (`r mc_test$n[mc_test$group == "Mexican"]`): `r gap_t("Mexican", "before")` to `r gap_t("Mexican", "after")`
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r}
#| label: multicalibration-fix-plot
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| dark: true
ggplot(mc_test, aes(y = fct_rev(group))) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = observed - 2 * se, xmax = observed + 2 * se), width = 0.25, orientation = "y", colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(x = observed, colour = "share with diabetes"), size = 3.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = predicted, colour = "average score, before"), shape = 17, size = 3.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = after, colour = "average score, after"), shape = 15, size = 3.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`share with diabetes` = "white", `average score, before` = m_orange, `average score, after` = v_green),
                      name = NULL, breaks = c("share with diabetes", "average score, before", "average score, after")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "test adults", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
:::

It fixes the gap the data can establish. A gap of 2 or 3 points in a group of a few hundred is within noise, and a shift fitted to it does not carry over

## {.inverse .center background-image="img/part4-ggcoef.png" background-size="cover" background-opacity="0.45" background-color="#440154"}

::: {.notes}
Compress: plots of a fitted model describe the model; partial dependence, ICE and Shapley values for any model; importance by permuting or leaving out.
Background: GGally::ggcoef(), a linear model's coefficients with intervals; for a forest there is no such table.
