### Part 3: interpreting the model

## One predictor at a time

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: we can change x_2 to see how the predictions vary, but what do we do with the other predictors?

Left: one slope answers the question everywhere. Right: the answer depends on where you stand (here on x_2 itself; with interactions, on the other predictors too). The options are on the next slide.
:::

**How does the model use one specific predictor, $x_2$, say?** For linear regression this is simple: its coefficient. With flexible models the answer changes depending on where you look in the input space

```{r}
#| label: one-predictor
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: 62%
#| fig-align: center
# A line and a quadratic, with tangents at two values of x2: one slope for the line, two for the curve.
one_models <- c("linear regression", "a flexible model")
one_f <- function(model, x) if_else(model == one_models[1], 1 + 0.8 * x, 0.4 + 0.6 * x^2)
one_pred <- expand_grid(model = factor(one_models, levels = one_models), x2 = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 101)) |>
  mutate(pred = one_f(model, x2))
one_tan <- expand_grid(model = factor(one_models, levels = one_models), x0 = c(-1.2, 1)) |>
  mutate(y0 = one_f(model, x0), slope = if_else(model == one_models[1], 0.8, 1.2 * x0))
ggplot(one_pred, aes(x2, pred)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.3, colour = v_dark) +
  geom_segment(data = one_tan, aes(x = x0 - 0.55, xend = x0 + 0.55, y = y0 - 0.55 * slope, yend = y0 + 0.55 * slope),
               colour = m_pink, linewidth = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = one_tan, aes(x0, y0), colour = m_pink, size = 3.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) + labs(x = "x2", y = "prediction") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

::: {.ask}
We can change $x_2$ to see how the predictions vary, but what do we do with the other predictors?
:::

## Partial dependence for any model (not just GAM)

```{r}
#| label: pd-helpers
#| include: false
pd_curve <- function(fit, d, v, grid) map_dbl(grid, function(t) { nd <- d; nd[[v]] <- t; mean(predict(fit, nd)) })
# The simulated interaction of the ensembles lecture: x1 enters only through its product with a function of x2.
f1 <- function(x) x^2
f2 <- function(x) cos(pi * x / 2)
df_int <- tibble(x1 = runif(2000, -1, 1), x2 = runif(2000, -4, 4)) |>
  mutate(y = f1(x1) * f2(x2) + rnorm(2000))
```

::: {.notes}
PDP_j(t) as in the notation table: set, leave, predict, average. Wording rule: ICE evaluates f-hat at a modified input that may match no plausible unit. If asked: it is the model's prediction there, not what would have happened to unit i (the causality seminar's note).
:::

Options for the other inputs: hold them fixed (at medians, say: `plotmo`'s default); average over them (partial dependence, `pdp`); one curve for each unit (individual conditional expectation, ICE)

Unit $i$'s inputs with input $j$ set to a value $t$, the others left as they are:
$$
\mathrm{ICE}_i(t) = \hat f(x_{i1}, \ldots, t, \ldots, x_{ip}), \qquad
\mathrm{PDP}_j(t) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \hat f(x_{i1}, \ldots, t, \ldots, x_{ip})
$$

Compute on a grid of $t$ values and plot the curve(s)

ICE evaluates $\hat f$ at a modified input, which may correspond to no plausible unit

## Does this forest use $x_1$? {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
Every input at every split (bagging); nodes under 50 not split. Flat, like the GAM's curve last time.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = df_sub)
```

```{r}
#| label: rf-pdp-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| out-width: 56%
#| fig-align: center
# The code shown above, on 100 of the 2,000 units, and the plot.
fit_rf <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df_int, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 50)
df_sub <- df_int |> slice_sample(n = 100) |> mutate(yhat.id = row_number(), sign = if_else(f2(x2) > 0, "positive", "negative"), strength = f2(x2)^4)
ice_x1 <- partial(fit_rf, pred.var = "x1", ice = TRUE, train = as.data.frame(df_sub[, c("x1", "x2")]), grid.resolution = 30) |>
  as_tibble() |> left_join(df_sub |> select(yhat.id, sign, strength), by = "yhat.id")
pdp_x1 <- ice_x1 |> group_by(x1) |> summarise(yhat = mean(yhat), .groups = "drop")
ice_ylim <- range(ice_x1$yhat)
ggplot(pdp_x1, aes(x1, yhat)) +
  geom_line(colour = "black", linewidth = 1.8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ice_ylim) + labs(x = "x1", y = "prediction")
```

The PDP: $x_1$ set, $x_2$ at each unit's value, predictions averaged over 100 units

## The forest's ICE curves

::: {.notes}
Left: what the pdp package draws. Right: the same curves, shaded by a function of x_2 that we know only because we simulated the data. Teal solid: cos(pi x_2 / 2) > 0; orange dashed: < 0. Only the ICE curves show the interaction.
:::

```{r}
#| label: rf-ice-plot
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center
# The same forest, curves and axes as on the last slide, with the ICE curves added: plain, then shaded by x2.
ice_plain <- ggplot(ice_x1, aes(x1, yhat)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = yhat.id), colour = "grey30", alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = pdp_x1, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.8) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ice_ylim) + labs(x = "x1", y = "prediction", title = "ICE curves and their average, the PDP")
ice_shaded <- ggplot(ice_x1, aes(x1, yhat)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = yhat.id, colour = sign, linetype = sign, alpha = strength), linewidth = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = pdp_x1, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(positive = v_teal, negative = m_orange)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(positive = "solid", negative = "dashed")) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.03, 0.75), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = ice_ylim) + labs(x = "x1", y = NULL, title = "the same curves, shaded by x2")
(ice_plain | ice_shaded) & theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))
```

Thin: one curve per unit (ICE). Right: solid where $\cos(\pi x_2/2) > 0$, dashed where it is negative, more opaque the larger $|\cos(\pi x_2/2)|$. The forest fitted the interaction, PDP hides it, and ICE might show it

## Every predictor at once {minutes="1"}

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: what if we have no one predictor of interest, and want to know how the model uses all of them?

Two answers follow: one prediction split among the inputs; one number per input for the whole model.
:::

::: {.ask}
What if we don't have one specific predictor of interest, but want to know how the model uses all the predictors?
:::

. . .

- For one prediction: split it among the inputs (**Shapley values**)
- For the whole model: one number for each input (**importance**)

## Shapley values

```{r}
#| label: shapley-forest
#| include: false
# Exact Shapley values for two inputs, on 300 units that are also the background data. v(S): the inputs in S at
# the unit's values, the other input at every background unit's value, the forest's predictions averaged.
sh_units <- df_int |> slice_sample(n = 300)
cross <- expand_grid(i = 1:300, j = 1:300) |>
  mutate(x1 = sh_units$x1[i], x2 = sh_units$x2[j]) |>
  mutate(pred = predict(fit_rf, pick(x1, x2)))
v1 <- cross |> group_by(i) |> summarise(v = mean(pred)) |> pull(v)          # x1 known: average over x2
v2 <- cross |> group_by(j) |> summarise(v = mean(pred)) |> pull(v)          # x2 known: average over x1
v0 <- mean(cross$pred); v12 <- predict(fit_rf, sh_units)
# The worked example: the unit with the largest true interaction term x1^2 cos(pi x2 / 2).
ex <- which.max(sh_units$x1^2 * f2(sh_units$x2))
# Its coalition values are shown to two decimals, and the shares are computed from the values as shown.
ex_v <- round(c(v0, v1[ex], v2[ex], v12[ex]), 2)
ex_phi <- c(0.5 * ((ex_v[2] - ex_v[1]) + (ex_v[4] - ex_v[3])), 0.5 * ((ex_v[3] - ex_v[1]) + (ex_v[4] - ex_v[2])))
f2d <- function(v) sprintf("%.2f", v)
fx <- function(v) if (abs(100 * v - round(100 * v)) < 1e-8) sprintf("%.2f", v) else sprintf("%.3f", v)   # every digit exact
f2p <- function(v) if (v < 0) sprintf("(%.2f)", v) else sprintf("%.2f", v)   # negatives in brackets inside a difference
```

::: {.notes}
Shapley's value from cooperative game theory. One unit of the simulated interaction, the same forest.
Efficiency: the two shares add up to the prediction minus the average prediction.
:::

Split a prediction among the inputs, $\hat f(\mathbf x_i) - v_i(\varnothing) = \phi_{i1} + \dots + \phi_{ip}$; $v_i(S)$ predicts from the inputs in $S$ only (usually: the others averaged over the data, as in partial dependence). For two inputs, adding $x_1$ in either order (for $p$, all $p!$ orders):
$$
\phi_{i1} = \tfrac12\Big[\big(v_i(\{1\}) - v_i(\varnothing)\big) + \big(v_i(\{1, 2\}) - v_i(\{2\})\big)\Big]
$$

The forest, one unit with $x_1 = `r f2d(sh_units$x1[ex])`$ and $x_2 = `r f2d(sh_units$x2[ex])`$:

| $v_i(\varnothing)$ | $v_i(\{1\})$ | $v_i(\{2\})$ | $v_i(\{1, 2\}) = \hat f(\mathbf x_i)$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `r f2d(ex_v[1])` | `r f2d(ex_v[2])` | `r f2d(ex_v[3])` | `r f2d(ex_v[4])` |

$\phi_{i1} = \frac12\big[(`r f2d(ex_v[2])` - `r f2p(ex_v[1])`) + (`r f2d(ex_v[4])` - `r f2p(ex_v[3])`)\big] = `r fx(ex_phi[1])`$

$\phi_{i2} = \frac12\big[(`r f2d(ex_v[3])` - `r f2p(ex_v[1])`) + (`r f2d(ex_v[4])` - `r f2p(ex_v[2])`)\big] = `r fx(ex_phi[2])`$; together `r fx(sum(ex_phi))` $= `r f2d(ex_v[4])` - `r f2p(ex_v[1])` = \hat f(\mathbf x_i) - v_i(\varnothing)$

## Shapley values for one adult {minutes="2"}

```{r}
#| label: rf-bp
#| include: false
# A forest for systolic blood pressure from nine inputs; BMI is weight / height^2, so three inputs are tied.
imp_inputs <- c("Age", "Gender", "Race1", "Weight", "Height", "BMI", "Pulse", "TotChol", "Poverty")
rf_bp <- randomForest(BPSysAve ~ Age + Gender + Race1 + Weight + Height + BMI + Pulse + TotChol + Poverty,
                      data = nh_train, ntree = 300, mtry = 3)
# Exact marginal Shapley values for 200 tuning adults (kernelshap::permshap, all 512 coalitions), with 50
# training adults as the background data.
shap_rows <- sample(nrow(nh_tune), 200)
shap_bp <- permshap(rf_bp, X = nh_tune[shap_rows, imp_inputs], bg_X = nh_train[sample(nrow(nh_train), 50), imp_inputs],
                    verbose = FALSE)
sv_bp <- shapviz(shap_bp)
shap_one <- which.max(predict(rf_bp, nh_tune[shap_rows, ]))   # the adult with the highest prediction of the 200
```

::: {.notes}
Marginal Shapley values (Chen et al.'s "true to the model"), exact: permshap evaluates all 2^9 coalitions, each averaged over 50 background adults. Bars: phi_ij; the sum is the last value minus the first.
:::

We now use the same NHANES adults to predict **systolic blood pressure** (mm Hg): a forest on nine inputs, fitted on the 4,000 training adults

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| label: waterfall-plot
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.3
sv_waterfall(sv_bp, row_id = shap_one, fill_colors = c(v_teal, m_pink), annotation_size = 5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) + labs(x = "prediction (mm Hg)", y = NULL)
```
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
A **waterfall plot** (SHAP: Lundberg and Lee 2017). It starts at the average prediction over the background adults, $v_i(\varnothing)$, adds each input's $\phi_{ij}$, largest first, and ends at this adult's prediction $\hat f(\mathbf x_i)$

The adult with the highest prediction of 200 tuning adults
:::
:::

## Feature/variable "importance"

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide (tree-specific and permutation importance), with LOCO added. IML: LOFO. The forest of the waterfall plot: systolic blood pressure, nine inputs, 300 trees, mtry = 3.
:::

- Which predictors are *used most* by the model? The forest for systolic blood pressure

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
#### Tree-specific importance [■]{style="color: #440154"}

Sum the RSS decrease of every split on $x_j$ within a tree, then average over trees

#### Permutation importance [▲]{style="color: #b73779"}

Permute values of predictor $x_j$. How much does the accuracy of the model decrease?
$$\mathrm{PI}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f, x_j \text{ permuted}) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)$$
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
#### Leave one covariate out [◆]{style="color: #31688e"}

Refit without input $j$, with the same settings; score on the same held-out adults (Lei et al. 2018):
$$\mathrm{LOCO}_j = \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}\big(\hat f^{(-j)}\big) - \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}(\hat f)$$

No extrapolation from permuting; any method, at the cost of $p$ refits
:::
:::

## Importance on the forest

```{r}
#| label: importance-calc
#| include: false
# Permutation importance on the tuning adults (ten shuffles), split improvement, mean |Shapley value| over the 200
# adults of the waterfall plot, and LOCO: the forest refitted without the input, scored on the tuning adults.
base_tune <- mse(nh_tune$BPSysAve, predict(rf_bp, nh_tune))
pi_j <- sapply(imp_inputs, function(v) mean(replicate(10, {
  d <- nh_tune; d[[v]] <- sample(d[[v]]); mse(nh_tune$BPSysAve, predict(rf_bp, d)) })) - base_tune)
split_j <- importance(rf_bp)[imp_inputs, "IncNodePurity"]
shap_j <- colMeans(abs(shap_bp$S))[imp_inputs]
# Leave one covariate out (three slides on): the forest refitted without the input, scored on the tuning adults.
refit_without <- function(drop) {
  fit <- randomForest(reformulate(setdiff(imp_inputs, drop), "BPSysAve"), data = nh_train, ntree = 300, mtry = 3)
  mse(nh_tune$BPSysAve, predict(fit, nh_tune)) - base_tune
}
loco_j <- sapply(imp_inputs, refit_without)
loco_body <- refit_without(c("Weight", "Height", "BMI"))
# Run-to-run noise: the full forest refitted five times with the same settings.
refit_sd <- sd(replicate(5, mse(nh_tune$BPSysAve, predict(randomForest(reformulate(imp_inputs, "BPSysAve"), data = nh_train,
                                                                          ntree = 300, mtry = 3), nh_tune))))
```

::: {.notes}
Each measure as a share of its own total, so the four scales differ. In MSE units LOCO is smaller than permutation for every input (age `r sprintf("%.0f", loco_j[["Age"]])` against `r sprintf("%.0f", pi_j[["Age"]])`): the refitted forest can use inputs correlated with the one left out. LOCO is even more concentrated on age than permutation, because the forest can do without any one of the other inputs. A LOCO share can be negative: refitting noise.
If asked about dependence: weight, height and BMI together `r sprintf("%.1f", loco_body)`; each alone `r sprintf("%.1f", loco_j[["Weight"]])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", loco_j[["Height"]])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", loco_j[["BMI"]])`; refitting the same forest moves its MSE by about `r sprintf("%.1f", refit_sd)` (sd, five refits). Any two give the third.
:::

```{r}
#| label: importance
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-align: center
tibble(input = factor(imp_inputs, levels = imp_inputs[order(split_j)]),
       `split improvement` = split_j / sum(split_j), permutation = pi_j / sum(pi_j), `mean |Shapley value|` = shap_j / sum(shap_j),
       LOCO = loco_j / sum(loco_j)) |>
  pivot_longer(-input, names_to = "measure") |>
  mutate(measure = fct_inorder(measure)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, input, colour = measure, shape = measure, size = measure)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`split improvement` = v_dark, permutation = m_pink, `mean |Shapley value|` = v_teal, LOCO = v_blue), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`split improvement` = 15, permutation = 17, `mean |Shapley value|` = 16, LOCO = 18), name = NULL) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(`split improvement` = 3.8, permutation = 3.8, `mean |Shapley value|` = 3.8, LOCO = 5), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "share of the measure's total", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right", axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15))
```

- Does not necessarily tell us about **causation** (none of these methods do)
- Each has pros/cons, no satisfactory answer for dependence

## Permutation with correlated inputs {.inverse}

```{r}
#| label: biv-perm
#| include: false
n_biv <- 400; rho_biv <- -0.8
b1 <- rnorm(n_biv); b2 <- rho_biv * b1 + sqrt(1 - rho_biv^2) * rnorm(n_biv)
biv <- tibble(x1 = b1, x2 = b2); biv_perm <- tibble(x1 = b1, x2 = sample(b2))
biv_lims <- c(-3.6, 3.6)
biv_kde <- MASS::kde2d(biv$x1, biv$x2, n = 120, lims = c(biv_lims, biv_lims))
biv_grid <- expand_grid(x2 = biv_kde$y, x1 = biv_kde$x) |> mutate(z = as.vector(t(biv_kde$z)))
biv_breaks <- c(0.002, 0.01, 0.03, 0.06, 0.1, 0.15, 0.3)
dens_at <- function(x, y) biv_kde$z[cbind(pmax(findInterval(x, biv_kde$x), 1), pmax(findInterval(y, biv_kde$y), 1))]
low_perm <- mean(dens_at(biv_perm$x1, biv_perm$x2) < 0.01); low_data <- mean(dens_at(biv$x1, biv$x2) < 0.01)
```

::: {.notes}
Compress: permuting one of two correlated inputs puts many points where the model has seen almost no data. x_1, x_2 standard normal with correlation -0.8; both panels shade the density estimated from the data on the left.
:::

```{r}
#| label: biv-perm-plot
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
#| dark: true
biv_panel <- function(d, title) ggplot() +
  geom_contour_filled(data = biv_grid, aes(x1, x2, z = z), breaks = biv_breaks, alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = d, aes(x1, x2), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako", direction = -1, begin = 0.15) +
  coord_equal(xlim = biv_lims, ylim = biv_lims, expand = FALSE) + labs(title = title, x = "x1", y = "x2") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17))
biv_panel(biv, "the data, and their density") + biv_panel(biv_perm, "x2 permuted, the same density")
```

Where the data's density is below 0.01: `r round(100 * low_perm)`% of the permuted points, `r round(100 * low_data)`% of the data

## Permutation and extrapolation

```{r}
#| label: permute-counts
#| include: false
# Height shuffled once among the tuning adults; weight and BMI stay. BMI from weight (kg) and height (cm).
perm <- nh_tune |> mutate(Height = sample(Height))
bmi_from <- function(d) d$Weight / (d$Height / 100)^2
off <- function(d) mean(abs(d$BMI - bmi_from(d)) > 2)
short_heavy <- function(d) sum(d$Height < 155 & d$Weight > 110)
```

::: {.notes}
Height shuffled once. Hooker, Mentch and Zhou (2021): shuffling puts weight where there are few data, in importance and partial dependence alike.
:::

```{r}
#| label: permute-height
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-align: center
bind_rows(nh_tune |> mutate(data = "tuning adults"),
          perm |> mutate(data = "height permuted")) |>
  mutate(data = fct_inorder(data), from = bmi_from(pick(everything()))) |>
  ggplot(aes(from, BMI)) + geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1, colour = v_blue) +
  facet_wrap(~ data) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10, 80), ylim = c(15, 70)) +
  labs(x = "weight / height squared", y = "recorded BMI") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 16))
```

Shuffling height keeps each adult's weight and BMI: BMI no longer matches weight and height for `r round(100 * off(perm))`% of them (`r round(100 * off(nh_tune))`% before); `r short_heavy(perm)` are under 155 cm and over 110 kg (`r short_heavy(nh_tune)` before)

The forest's predictions there rest on almost no data, and permutation importance averages over them (Hooker, Mentch and Zhou 2021)

## {.inverse .center background-image="img/part5-sachs-ecm.png" background-size="cover" background-opacity="0.5" background-color="#440154"}

::: {.notes}
Compress: a plot of the model answers a question about the model; a question about the world needs a causal model and a model that is right about the world.
Background: the ECM of Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), Figure 5, for the protein-signalling data of Sachs et al. (2005).
:::

### Part 4: the model and the world

[Background: after Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), Figure 5]{style="font-size: 0.5em; color: #e5e5e5"}

## Predictions and outcomes {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: world
#| include: false
# The world of this part (simulated): x1 causes x2; both cause y; x3 is caused by x1 and by y (a collider).
n_w <- 2000
x2_eq <- function(x1) x1 + rnorm(length(x1), 0, 0.8)
y_eq  <- function(x1, x2) 0.5 * x1 + 1.5 * sin(x2) + rnorm(length(x1), 0, 0.5)
x3_eq <- function(x1, y) y + x1 + rnorm(length(x1), 0, 0.3)
draw_world <- function(n) tibble(x1 = runif(n, -2, 2)) |> mutate(x2 = x2_eq(x1), y = y_eq(x1, x2), x3 = x3_eq(x1, y))
world <- draw_world(n_w); world_fresh <- draw_world(n_w)
# The fitted model: a forest on x1, x2 and x3; and a forest on x1 and x2, for the test MSE in the notes.
fit_w <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = world, ntree = 300, mtry = 3, nodesize = 20)
fit_w12 <- randomForest(y ~ x1 + x2, data = world, ntree = 300, mtry = 2, nodesize = 20)
mse_w <- c(mse(world_fresh$y, predict(fit_w, world_fresh)), mse(world_fresh$y, predict(fit_w12, world_fresh)))
```

::: {.notes}
QUESTION: to let x_2 and x_3 respond when we change x_1, what do we need besides the fitted model?

A causal model for the inputs, and here for y as well, since x_3 depends on y. Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), Definition 2.5; drawn as in their Figure 5.
2,000 simulated units; test MSE `r sprintf("%.2f", mse_w[1])` with x_3, `r sprintf("%.2f", mse_w[2])` without.
:::

::: {.ask}
A partial dependence plot for $x_1$ leaves $x_2$ and $x_3$ at each unit's value. In the world, they respond to $x_1$. To let them respond, what do we need besides the fitted model?
:::

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
A causal model for the inputs. An **explanatory causal model** (ECM; Loftus, Bynum and Hansen 2024) adds the prediction $\hat Y = \hat f(X)$, with dashed arrows from the model's inputs. Here $x_3$ depends on $y$, so $y$ is in it too:

$x_2 = x_1 + \varepsilon_2$, $\ y = \tfrac12 x_1 + \tfrac32 \sin x_2 + \varepsilon$, $\ x_3 = y + x_1 + \varepsilon_3$; $\hat f$, a forest on $x_1, x_2, x_3$
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r}
#| label: ecm-plot
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
ecm_plot()
```
:::
:::

## Natural direct and total dependence {minutes="3"}

```{r}
#| label: tdp
#| include: false
t_grid <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 41)
avg_pred <- mean(predict(fit_w, world))
nddp <- pd_curve(fit_w, world, "x1", t_grid)
# Total dependence: set x1 to t for every unit, draw x2, y and x3 again from their equations, predict, average.
tdp <- map_dbl(t_grid, function(t) {
  d <- tibble(x1 = rep(t, n_w)) |> mutate(x2 = x2_eq(x1), y = y_eq(x1, x2), x3 = x3_eq(x1, y))
  mean(predict(fit_w, d))
})
# The effect of setting x1 on y, from the equations: E[sin(t + e2)] = sin(t) exp(-0.8^2 / 2), and E[Y] = 0.
eff_x1 <- 0.5 * t_grid + 1.5 * sin(t_grid) * exp(-0.8^2 / 2)
# Marginal Shapley values for x1 on 300 units, with 200 others as the background (exact for three inputs).
sh_w <- permshap(fit_w, X = world[1:300, c("x1", "x2", "x3")], bg_X = world[301:500, c("x1", "x2", "x3")], verbose = FALSE)
```

::: {.notes}
Their Definitions 2.9 and 2.7; PDP with ICE = NDDP is Theorem 2.10. Curves minus the average prediction; dashed: E[Y | do(x_1 = t)] from the equations.
TDP on the effect: x_1 has no parents, so do(x_1 = t) is conditioning on x_1 = t, and E[f*(X) | x_1 = t] = E[Y | x_1 = t] (tower property); here f-hat is close to f*.
:::

In the ECM, set $x_1 = t$ for every unit, predict, average, with $x_2$ and $x_3$

- left at each unit's value: the **natural direct dependence plot** (NDDP), which is the PDP
- recomputed from their equations: the **total dependence plot** (TDP), $\mathbb E[\hat f(X) \mid do(x_1 = t)]$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: tdp-plot
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 2.6
dep <- tibble(t = t_grid, NDDP = nddp - avg_pred, TDP = tdp - avg_pred, effect = eff_x1) |>
  pivot_longer(-t, names_to = "curve") |> mutate(curve = fct_inorder(curve))
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = tibble(x1 = world$x1[1:300], phi = sh_w$S[, "x1"]), aes(x1, phi), colour = "grey45", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = dep, aes(t, value, colour = curve, linetype = curve), linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(NDDP = m_pink, TDP = v_blue, effect = "black"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(NDDP = "solid", TDP = "solid", effect = "dashed"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "x1", y = "centered") + theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 17), legend.key.width = unit(1.6, "lines"))
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
NDDP falls: with $x_3$ held fixed, a larger $x_1$ means a smaller $y$. TDP follows the effect of setting $x_1$ (dashed). Grey: Shapley values for $x_1$

**Causal Shapley values** (Heskes et al. 2020) put $do(\cdot)$ in place of conditioning
:::
:::

## Partial dependence and causal effects

::: {.notes}
A heuristic; no statement to learn. First bullet: Zhao and Hastie (2021): the PDP is the adjustment formula with the model in place of the regression function. It also needs overlap, as in the causality lecture. Second bullet: Loftus, Bynum and Hansen (2024), Theorem 2.10: PDP = NDDP.
The formal statement (the model-intervention corollary) is not set; the notebook's coding part 2 shows the failures.
The first is a claim about the world, and needs assumptions about the world. The second is about the model.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
- If the **adjustment theorem's assumptions hold**, with the plotted input as $T$ and the model's other inputs as $Z$, and the **model fits the true regression function well**, then the PDP can show the causal effect of $T$ on the outcome (Zhao and Hastie 2021)
- Whatever the causal structure, the PDP shows the natural direct effect of the plotted input **on the predicted outcome** $\hat Y$ (Loftus, Bynum and Hansen 2024)

:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
```{r}
#| label: corollary-dag
#| fig-width: 3.6
#| fig-height: 3.3
dag_adjust(FALSE, "as observed") / dag_adjust(TRUE, "under do(T = t)")
```
:::
:::

::: {.retrieval}
Adjustment theorem: $Z$ holds every common cause of $T$ and $Y$, and no consequence of $T$
:::

## Conclusion {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
Compress: the loss decides the target; check intervals and probabilities on fresh data and across the range; a plot of the model describes the model, and an effect needs a causal model and a model that is right.
:::

#### Uncertainty

The loss decides which number is the best prediction; the pinball loss gives a quantile. Residuals from held-out rows give an interval that covers 90% on average, for any model. Coverage at every $x$ needs edges fitted near $x$, enough rows there, and assumptions: no method guarantees it in finite samples without them. Check coverage and calibration on data not used to fit or tune, across the range of the inputs and within groups

#### Interpretation

Partial dependence, ICE, Shapley values and importance describe $\hat f$. If the adjustment theorem's assumptions hold and the model fits well, the PDP can show a causal effect; with a causal model for the inputs, the total dependence plot answers a different question

## Conformalized quantile regression {.inverse minutes="0"}

```{r}
#| label: cqr
#| include: false
# Boosted 5% and 95% fits on the first 500 training points; scores on the other 500 (m = 500).
fit_part <- 1:500; cal_part <- 501:1000
m_cal <- length(cal_part); k90 <- ceiling(0.9 * (m_cal + 1))
boost_half <- function(tau) xgboost(x = as.matrix(het_train[fit_part, "x"]), y = het_train$y[fit_part],
  objective = "reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha = tau,
  max_depth = 2, learning_rate = 0.05, nrounds = 300, min_child_weight = 30, nthread = 1)
b05_half <- boost_half(0.05); b95_half <- boost_half(0.95)
plug_in <- function(d) cbind(predict(b05_half, as.matrix(d["x"])), predict(b95_half, as.matrix(d["x"])))
cal <- het_train[cal_part, ]
b_cal <- plug_in(cal)
cal$score <- pmax(b_cal[, 1] - cal$y, cal$y - b_cal[, 2])
Q_cqr <- sort(cal$score)[k90]
b_fresh <- plug_in(het_fresh)
in_plug <- het_fresh$y >= b_fresh[, 1] & het_fresh$y <= b_fresh[, 2]
in_cqr <- het_fresh$y >= b_fresh[, 1] - Q_cqr & het_fresh$y <= b_fresh[, 2] + Q_cqr
in_46 <- het_fresh$x >= 4 & het_fresh$x < 6
b_own <- plug_in(het_train[fit_part, ])
cover_own <- mean(het_train$y[fit_part] >= b_own[, 1] & het_train$y[fit_part] <= b_own[, 2])
```

::: {.notes}
Skip unless asked: the conformal correction applied to two quantile fits, so the interval keeps their shape. One calibration set of 500: coverage varies by about 1.3 points (sd) between sets.
Romano, Patterson and Candès (2019), section 4, equations 6 to 8. The fits cover `r pct(cover_own)` of their own points, `r pct(mean(cal$score <= 0))` of the calibration rows: Q > 0.
Why, if asked: the new row's score has a uniform rank among the m + 1. Sesia and Candès (2020), Theorem 1 and its corollary, also need the scores to have a density bounded away from zero near zero.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
1. Fit $\hat q_{0.05}$, $\hat q_{0.95}$ on some training rows; keep $m$ others, the **calibration set**
2. Score how far each $y_i$ is outside (negative inside): $E_i = \max\{\hat q_{0.05}(x_i) - y_i,\ y_i - \hat q_{0.95}(x_i)\}$
3. $Q$: the $\lceil 0.9\,(m + 1) \rceil$-th smallest score
4. $\hat C(x) = \big[\hat q_{0.05}(x) - Q,\ \hat q_{0.95}(x) + Q\big]$
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
```{r}
#| label: cqr-plot
#| fig-width: 4.3
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| dark: true
ggplot(cal, aes(x, score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = score > Q_cqr), size = 1.3, alpha = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = Q_cqr, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9, colour = "white") +
  annotate("text", x = 10, y = Q_cqr, label = "Q", size = 5.5, hjust = -0.6, colour = "white") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey80", `TRUE` = m_orange)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "score") + theme(plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(5, 30, 5, 5))
```

$m = `r m_cal`$, $Q = `r sprintf("%.2f", Q_cqr)`$: `r pct(mean(in_plug))` to `r pct(mean(in_cqr))`; for $x$ in 4–6, `r pct(mean(in_plug[in_46]))` to `r pct(mean(in_cqr[in_46]))`
:::
:::

::: {.leave}
**The conformal coverage theorem holds for any quantile fits** (Romano et al. 2019): $P(Y \in \hat C(X)) \ge 0.9$, and $\le 0.9 + 1/(m + 1)$ for continuous scores. If the fits are consistent, $Q \to 0$ and coverage at every $x$ approaches 90% (Sesia and Candès 2020)
:::

## Exchangeable rows and atoms {.inverse minutes="0"}

::: {.notes}
Skip: for students who ask about the assumptions.
:::

These slides state two conditions more simply than the sources do:

- **Exchangeable rows.** The conformal coverage theorem (Lei et al. 2018; Romano et al. 2019, Theorem 1) needs only rows $(X_1, Y_1), \dots, (X_{m+1}, Y_{m+1})$ whose joint distribution is unchanged when they are reordered: **exchangeable** rows. Independent draws from one distribution are exchangeable; draws without replacement from a finite population are exchangeable but not independent.
- **Atoms.** The impossibility theorem (Barber et al. 2021, Proposition 2.2) is about each $x$ that is not an **atom**, a value with positive probability; continuous inputs have no atoms. The upper bound $1 - \alpha + 1/(m + 1)$ needs only scores that are distinct with probability one
- Sesia and Candès (2020) do assume independent rows from one distribution
